pos: n. (proper, the greatest of the Anakims; Hebrew, four)
etymology: Hebrew Arba, four. He gave his name to Kirjath-arba, the city of Arba, which Israel afterwards called Hebron — the place of Abraham's grave and of David's first throne.
biblical_def: Joshua tells us who he was in an aside: “And the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba; which Arba was a great man among the Anakims. And the land had rest from war” (Joshua 14:15). The verse before it records Caleb receiving Hebron for an inheritance at eighty-five, because he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel. Twice more the city is described by the man: Caleb was given “the city of Arba the father of Anak, which city is Hebron” (Joshua 15:13), and the priests received “the city of Arba the father of Anak, which city is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, with the suburbs thereof” (Joshua 21:11). The ten spies had come back from this very place saying they were as grasshoppers in the sight of the Anakims. Forty-five years later the old man who had said we are well able to overcome it asked for that mountain and took it, and a city named after a giant became a city of refuge and of priests.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a great man among the Anakims, the father of Anak, whose city Kirjath-arba became Hebron.
webster_full: ANAKIM, n. In Scripture, a race of giants who dwelt in the hill country of Canaan, especially about Hebron.
GIANT, n. A man of extraordinary bulk and stature; in Scripture, one of a race of unusual size and strength.
HEBRON, n. An ancient city of Judah in the hill country, the burial place of the patriarchs and David's first capital.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; in Israel, a city appointed for the manslayer to flee to.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir; in Scripture, the portion of a tribe or family in the land.
scriptures: Joshua 14:15
And the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba; which Arba was a great man among the Anakims. And the land had rest from war.
Joshua 15:13
And unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh he gave a part among the children of Judah, according to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, even the city of Arba the father of Anak, which city is Hebron. the
Joshua 21:11
And they gave them the city of Arba the father of Anak, which city is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, with the suburbs thereof round about it. the
Joshua 14:12

Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day; for thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced: if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out, as the LORD said.
corruption_summary: Obstacles are sized up by the resources of the one facing them, which is exactly the arithmetic of the ten spies; Caleb measured the same giants against the promise of God and asked for their mountain at eighty-five.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 13 and Joshua 14 describe the same city and reach opposite conclusions. The ten spies reported walled cities, great and tall men, the children of Anak, and said we be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we. Caleb saw the identical giants and said the identical facts and added one more: the LORD is with us. The difference was not optimism against pessimism but arithmetic with God left out against arithmetic with God in. Forty-five years later he was still asking for that hill: Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day.

The result is worth sitting with. A city named for the greatest of the Anakims became Hebron, the burial place of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, a city of refuge for the manslayer, a priests' city, and the place where David reigned seven years before Jerusalem. The stronghold of a giant was turned into a sanctuary for the weak. That reversal is the pattern of redemption in miniature, and it began with one old man who wholly followed the LORD when everyone else did the sums without him.
roots_summary: Hebrew Arba (H704), four; Qiryath Arba (H7153), city of Arba; Anaq (H6061), Anak, long-necked; Chebrown (H2275), Hebron, fellowship.
roots_lines: Hebrew Arba (H704) — Arba, four; a great man among the Anakims.
Hebrew Qiryath Arba (H7153) — Kirjath-arba, the city of Arba; Hebron's older name.
Hebrew Anaq (H6061) — Anak, long-necked; the giant stock that terrified the ten spies.
Hebrew Chebrown (H2275) — Hebron, from chabar, to join; association or fellowship.
Hebrew male achar — to fill up after, to wholly follow; said of Caleb five times.
usage: “Which Arba was a great man among the Anakims” — the city's namesake.
“The city of Arba the father of Anak, which city is Hebron”.
“Now therefore give me this mountain” — Caleb at eighty-five.

pos: n. (proper, one of the three sons of Anak)
etymology: Hebrew Sheshay, probably whitish or noble. He is named three times, always with his two brothers Ahiman and Talmai, and always in connection with Hebron.
biblical_def: The twelve spies met them: “And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)” (Numbers 13:22). Forty-five years later the same three are driven out by one man: “And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak” (Joshua 15:14). And at the opening of Judges the tribe finishes the work: “And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai” (Judges 1:10). Scripture names all three men in all three passages. The giants who made ten spies feel like grasshoppers are not left as a vague terror; they are named, counted, located and finally killed, and the record of their defeat is as specific as the record of the fear they caused.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the three sons of Anak who dwelt in Hebron and were driven out by Caleb.
webster_full: ANAK, n. The progenitor of the Anakim, a race of giants in the hill country of Canaan.
GRASSHOPPER, n. An insect of the genus Gryllus; in Scripture, a figure of smallness and insignificance.
SPY, n. A person sent into an enemy's camp or country to inspect their works, ascertain their strength and designs.
TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind.
CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the act of overcoming or vanquishing opposition by force.
scriptures: Numbers 13:22
And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)
Joshua 15:14
And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
Judges 1:10
And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai.
Numbers 13:33
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
corruption_summary: Fear works by keeping its objects vague and enormous; Scripture names the three giants, notes where they lived, and then records exactly who killed them and when.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 13:33 is the classic description of how fear distorts a report: And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight. Notice the last clause. The spies did not merely report the giants' size; they reported the giants' opinion of them, which no one had told them. Fear supplies the other side's thoughts and then treats the invention as intelligence. It is worth saying plainly because the habit is universal, and it kept a generation out of the land.

The corrective in the text is the naming. Ahiman, Sheshai, Talmai — three men, not a legend; living in Hebron, not everywhere; and in Joshua 15 driven out by an eighty-five-year-old, and in Judges 1 slain by Judah. Scripture keeps the same three names across three books so that the reader who trembled in Numbers can see the account closed. Bring a fear into the light, count it, name it and set it beside the promise of God, and it has already lost the part of its power that came from being vague.
roots_summary: Hebrew Sheshay (H8344), whitish or noble; Achiyman (H289), Ahiman; Talmay (H8526), Talmai; chagab (H2284), a grasshopper.
roots_lines: Hebrew Sheshay (H8344) — Sheshai, one of the three sons of Anak at Hebron.
Hebrew Achiyman (H289) — Ahiman, brother of a gift; named with him in all three passages.
Hebrew Talmay (H8526) — Talmai, furrowed; the third brother.
Hebrew Nephiyl (H5303) — the giants, the fallen ones; the stock the spies reported.
Hebrew chagab (H2284) — a grasshopper; the spies' estimate of themselves.
usage: “Where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were”.
“Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak” — one man, three giants.
“They slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai” — the account closed.

pos: n. (proper, an Amorite confederate of Abram; also a Levitical city)
etymology: Hebrew Aner, of uncertain meaning. He was one of three Amorite brothers in the plain of Mamre who were confederate with Abram, and a city of the same name was afterwards given to the Levites.
biblical_def: When Lot was carried off by the four kings, the report came to a man with allies: “And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram” (Genesis 14:13). They went with him in the night pursuit as far as Dan and Hobah. Afterwards the king of Sodom offered Abram the goods, and Abram refused — he had lifted his hand unto the LORD that he would not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, lest Sodom should say it had made him rich — but he made an exception he had no right to impose on other men: “Save only that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men which went with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre; let them take their portion” (Genesis 14:24). A city Aner is later given to the Kohathites out of the half tribe of Manasseh (1 Chronicles 6:70).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as an Amorite, brother of Mamre and Eshcol, confederate with Abram, and as a Levitical city of Manasseh.
webster_full: CONFEDERATE, a. United in a league; allied by treaty; as, confederate states or princes.
AMORITE, n. One of a people of Canaan, dwelling in the mountains, descended from Amor the son of Canaan.
ALLY, n. A prince or state united by treaty or league; a confederate.
SCRUPLE, n. Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right; a nice regard to exact propriety.
PORTION, n. A part of anything separated from the whole; the part of an estate assigned to an heir.
scriptures: Genesis 14:13
And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram.
Genesis 14:24
Save only that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men which went with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre; let them take their portion.
1 Chronicles 6:70
And out of the half tribe of Manasseh; Aner with her suburbs, and Bileam with her suburbs, for the family of the remnant of the sons of Kohath.
Genesis 14:23
That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that is thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich:
corruption_summary: Personal convictions are commonly imposed on others as though they were commands of God; Abram took nothing from Sodom because of a vow he had made, and expressly left Aner, Eshcol and Mamre free to take their portion.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 14:24 is a small masterpiece of Christian liberty and it is routinely overlooked. Abram had sworn an oath — I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth, that I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet — and he kept it absolutely, for a reason he states: lest the king of Sodom should say, I have made Abram rich. And then, in the same breath, he refuses to bind Aner, Eshcol and Mamre by his own vow. Let them take their portion. They had fought; the portion was justly theirs; his scruple was his own.

Paul works this out at length in Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8. A believer may abstain from a lawful thing for conscience' sake, for testimony, or because of a vow, and he is right to do so. What he may not do is legislate his abstinence for the church or despise the brother who eats. The line Abram draws — strict with himself, generous with his allies — is exactly the line a great deal of modern Christian controversy fails to draw, in both directions: the rigorist binding others, and the liberty-taker despising the scrupulous.
roots_summary: Hebrew Aner (H6063); Mamre (H4471), fatness; Eshkol (H812), a cluster; baal beriyth, a master of covenant, hence confederate.
roots_lines: Hebrew Aner (H6063) — Aner; an Amorite confederate with Abram, and a Levitical city.
Hebrew Mamre (H4471) — Mamre, fatness or vigour; his brother, and the plain Abram dwelt in.
Hebrew Eshkol (H812) — Eshcol, a cluster; the third brother.
Hebrew baaley beriyth — masters of a covenant; the AV's confederate with Abram.
Hebrew serowk naal — a shoelatchet; the smallest thing Abram would not take.
usage: “These were confederate with Abram” — a believing man had allies.
“Let them take their portion” — his vow was not laid on them.
“From a thread even to a shoelatchet” — how strictly he kept his own.

pos: n. (proper, king of Hamath; also written Tou)
etymology: Hebrew Toiy, error or wandering; the Chronicler spells it Tou. He was king of Hamath on the Orontes, and the only foreign king in the books of Samuel who comes to David with a blessing rather than a sword.
biblical_def: After David's campaign against Zobah the news travelled north: “When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer” (2 Samuel 8:9), “Then Toi sent Joram his son unto king David, to salute him, and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer, and smitten him: for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. And Joram brought with him vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and vessels of brass” (2 Samuel 8:10). The Chronicler records the same embassy: “Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah” (1 Chronicles 18:9), and the historian notes the end of the treasure — David dedicated it unto the LORD with the silver and gold of all the nations he subdued. The motive named is frank: for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. A common enemy made the friendship, and God turned a political gift into temple silver.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the king of Hamath who sent his son to salute and bless David, also written Tou.
webster_full: HAMATH, n. A city and kingdom of upper Syria on the Orontes, the northern boundary of Israel at her greatest extent.
EMBASSY, n. The message or public function of an ambassador; the person or persons sent as ambassadors.
SALUTE, v.t. To greet; to hail; to address with expressions of kind wishes.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another.
DEDICATE, v.t. To set apart and consecrate to a divine Being, or to a sacred purpose.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 8:9
When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer,
2 Samuel 8:10

Then Toi sent Joram his son unto king David, to salute him, and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer, and smitten him: for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. And Joram brought with him vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and vessels of brass:
1 Chronicles 18:9
Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; Tou: also called, Toi
2 Samuel 8:11
Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD, with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued;
corruption_summary: Alliances of convenience are either condemned outright as compromise or trusted as friendships; Scripture states Toi's motive plainly and records that David took the gift and dedicated it unto the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The instructive thing is the candour of the record. Toi sent his son to salute and to bless David, and the historian adds, without embarrassment, for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. Scripture does not pretend the embassy was disinterested affection. Nations act from interest, and a common enemy is a common interest. A believer who expects the world's goodwill to rest on anything else will be repeatedly disappointed; one who understands what it rests on can receive it gratefully and hold it loosely.

What David did with the gift is the point that lifts the episode. 2 Samuel 8:11 records that he dedicated the vessels unto the LORD, with the silver and gold he had dedicated of all the nations he subdued. The spoils of politics became the furniture of worship, and the chronicler notes elsewhere that David gathered such material for the house his son would build. The principle to recover is neither isolation from the world's dealings nor entanglement in them, but the habit of taking whatever God gives through them and consecrating it to him.
roots_summary: Hebrew Toiy (H8583), error; Tou (H8583), the Chronicler's spelling; Chamath (H2574), Hamath; qadash (H6942), to dedicate or sanctify.
roots_lines: Hebrew Toiy (H8583) — Toi, king of Hamath; the Chronicler writes Tou.
Hebrew Chamath (H2574) — Hamath; a Syrian kingdom on the Orontes.
Hebrew Hadadezer (H1909) — Hadadezer of Zobah, the enemy of both David and Toi.
Hebrew barak (H1288) — to bless, to kneel; Toi sent his son to bless David.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to consecrate; David dedicated the vessels unto the LORD.
usage: “Toi sent Joram his son unto king David, to salute him, and to bless him”.
“For Hadadezer had wars with Toi” — the motive stated plainly.
“Which also king David did dedicate unto the LORD” — what became of it.

pos: n. (proper, rival claimant to the throne of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew Tibniy, from teben, straw or chaff. The name of a man who divided a kingdom for several years and lost, and whose whole record in Scripture is two verses.
biblical_def: After Zimri's seven-day reign ended in the burning palace at Tirzah, the northern kingdom split: “Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king; and half followed Omri” (1 Kings 16:21). The outcome is given in one sentence: “But the people that followed Omri prevailed against the people that followed Tibni the son of Ginath: so Tibni died, and Omri reigned” (1 Kings 16:22). No cause of death is stated, no burial noted, no epitaph given. That is the whole of Tibni. And the man who beat him is worse — the record of Omri is that he wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD and did worse than all that were before him, and his son was Ahab. A civil war fought by two halves of a nation, with no word from a prophet on either side, produced the dynasty of Ahab and Jezebel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the son of Ginath, whom half of Israel followed to make him king against Omri.
webster_full: STRAW, n. The stalk or stem of certain species of grain, pulse, etc., chiefly of wheat, rye, oats and barley.
CHAFF, n. The husk or dry calyx of corn and grasses; in Scripture, a figure of the worthless and the transient.
USURPER, n. One who seizes or occupies the power or property of another without right.
FACTION, n. A party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the prince or state.
AMBITION, n. A desire of preferment or honor; a desire of superiority or distinction.
scriptures: 1 Kings 16:21
Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king; and half followed Omri.
1 Kings 16:22
But the people that followed Omri prevailed against the people that followed Tibni the son of Ginath: so Tibni died, and Omri reigned.
1 Kings 16:25
But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him.
Psalm 1:4
The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.
corruption_summary: Political contest is treated as the great arena of human significance, and Scripture disposes of a years-long civil war in two verses, then records that the winner was worse than every king before him.
corruption_paragraphs: Half a nation followed Tibni. Men died for it, families divided over it, and it lasted years. The Holy Ghost gives it two verses and does not tell us how Tibni died. The proportion is the message. Scripture is not indifferent to government — it devotes whole books to kings and gives elaborate laws for judges — but it consistently refuses to treat the contest for power as the thing of ultimate weight. A man whose sense of significance rises and falls with a political outcome is measuring by a scale the Bible does not use.

The sharper point is the winner. But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him. His house gave Israel Ahab, and Ahab gave Israel Jezebel and the priests of Baal. The victorious faction carried a nation further from God than the losing one could have. His name means straw, and the psalm says the ungodly are like the chaff which the wind driveth away. A believer may and should care about who governs; he may never conclude that the side which prevails is the side God favours.

pos: n. (proper, father of Barak; Hebrew, my father is pleasantness)
etymology: Hebrew Abiynoam, from ab, father, and noam, pleasantness or beauty — my father is delight. He is known only as the father of Barak, and the phrase Barak the son of Abinoam is repeated four times in two chapters.
biblical_def: Deborah sends for him by his full name: “And she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedeshnaphtali, and said unto him, Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor” (Judges 4:6). The enemy learns the same: “And they shewed Sisera that Barak the son of Abinoam was gone up to mount Tabor” (Judges 4:12). And when the battle is over, the song begins with the two of them: “Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day” (Judges 5:1). Barak's famous hesitation — If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go — cost him the honour of the day, which went to Jael. Yet Hebrews 11 lists Barak among the men who through faith subdued kingdoms. Abinoam is remembered for one thing: a son who, for all his faltering, went.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the father of Barak of Kedesh-naphtali, named four times in Judges 4 and 5.
webster_full: PATRONYMIC, n. A name derived from that of a father or ancestor; as, Barak the son of Abinoam.
DEBORAH, n. A prophetess who judged Israel and sang with Barak the song of Judges 5.
PLEASANTNESS, n. State of being pleasant; cheerfulness; gaiety; the quality of giving delight.
FALTER, v.i. To hesitate; to fail in resolution; to be feeble and irresolute.
VALOUR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; that quality which enables a man to encounter danger with firmness.
scriptures: Judges 4:6

And she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedeshnaphtali, and said unto him, Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?
Judges 4:12
And they shewed Sisera that Barak the son of Abinoam was gone up to mount Tabor.
Judges 5:1
Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day, saying,
Judges 4:8
And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go.
corruption_summary: Faith is imagined as an untroubled confidence, so that hesitation disqualifies; Barak bargained with a prophetess, lost the glory of the day, and is named in Hebrews 11 among the heroes of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 4:8 records a reply no one would put in a hero's mouth: If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go. Deborah answered that the journey he took would not be for his honour, for the LORD would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. Barak received a plain command from God through a prophetess and haggled. Scripture records the haggling and the cost of it, which is itself a mercy to every believer who has obeyed with a shake in his voice.

And then Hebrews 11:32 lists him: Gedeon, and Barak, and Samson, and Jephthae. The New Testament's roll of faith is not a roll of the unwavering. What God saw in Barak was that, having said what he said, he went up to Tabor with ten thousand men and fought. Faith in Scripture is not the absence of fear but obedience in the presence of it, and the honour a hesitating man forfeits is not the same as the salvation he keeps. Abinoam's name means my father is pleasantness; his son's record is a pleasant one only because God is kind to imperfect obedience.
roots_summary: Hebrew Abiynoam (H42), my father is pleasantness; Baraq (H1301), lightning; Qedesh (H6943), Kedesh, a sanctuary; Debowrah (H1683), Deborah, a bee.

“Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day”.

pos: n. (proper, father of Joshua the high priest; Hebrew, the LORD is righteous)
etymology: Hebrew Yehowtsadaq, Jehovah is righteous — the AV renders it Josedech in Haggai and Zechariah, Jehozadak in Chronicles. He was carried away to Babylon when the LORD removed Judah by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
biblical_def: The word of the LORD by Haggai came to two men: “In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest” (Haggai 1:1). The message was that the people dwelt in cieled houses while God's house lay waste. It worked: “And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the LORD of hosts” (Haggai 1:14). Later the prophet has to steady them: “Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel... and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you” (Haggai 2:4). Zechariah 3 shows the same Joshua standing before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, and clothed with change of raiment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the father of Joshua the high priest of the restoration, also written Jehozadak.
webster_full: HIGH PRIEST, n. The chief priest among the Hebrews, who alone entered the holy of holies, and that once a year.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
CIELED, pp. Overlaid or covered with thin boards, as the inside of a room; wainscoted.
GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority to administer a colony or province.
IMPUTATION, n. In theology, the attributing of the righteousness of Christ to a believer, or of sin to Christ.
scriptures: Haggai 1:1

In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying,
Haggai 1:14

And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they came and did work in the house of the LORD of hosts, their God,
Haggai 2:4

Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts:
Zechariah 3:4

And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.
corruption_summary: Worship is postponed until private affairs are settled — God's house waste while men live in cieled houses — and the priest who was to lead it stood before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments.
corruption_paragraphs: Haggai's charge is the most quietly devastating diagnosis of misplaced priority in the prophets: Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste? The people had not renounced the temple; they had deferred it, which is how the house of God is usually neglected. They then wondered why they sowed much and brought in little, and ate but had not enough. The remedy was not a change of principle but a change of calendar: go up to the mountain, bring wood, build the house. Twenty-three days later they were working.

Zechariah 3 shows what stood behind the failure and how it was answered. Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, the very man charged with the nation's worship, stands before the angel of the LORD clothed with filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to resist him. The Lord rebukes Satan, takes away the filthy garments and says, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment. That is the gospel in the plainest Old Testament picture there is, and it is given to a man whose father's name means the LORD is righteous. The righteousness in the name is the righteousness he had to be given.

pos: n. (proper, a descendant of Benjamin; Hebrew, fugitive or descent)
etymology: Hebrew Ard, probably a fugitive or one who descends. He is listed among Benjamin's house going down into Egypt, and heads the family of the Ardites in the wilderness census.
biblical_def: He appears in the roll of Jacob's household entering Egypt: “And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21). By the second census he is reckoned a generation further down and heads a clan: “And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the family of the Ardites: and of Naaman, the family of the Naamites” (Numbers 26:40). The Chronicler's list gives the name in another form, with the margin noting the variation (1 Chronicles 8:3). Benjamin is the tribe that was nearly destroyed in the civil war at the end of Judges, reduced to six hundred men at the rock Rimmon; and it is the tribe of Saul, of Mordecai, and of the apostle Paul, who called himself a Hebrew of the Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a descendant of Benjamin, head of the family of the Ardites.
webster_full: BENJAMIN, n. The youngest son of Jacob, and the tribe descended from him, the smallest of the tribes of Israel.
CENSUS, n. An official enumeration of the inhabitants of a state or nation, with their property.
CLAN, n. A race; a family; a tribe; particularly, a number of families united under a chieftain.
FUGITIVE, n. One who flees from his station or duty; one who takes refuge in another country.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation or destruction of a part.
scriptures: Genesis 46:21
And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard.
Numbers 26:40
And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the family of the Ardites: and of Naaman, the family of the Naamites.
1 Chronicles 8:3
And the sons of Bela were, Addar, and Gera, and Abihud,
Philippians 3:5
Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;
corruption_summary: A family or a people written off after catastrophe is assumed to be finished; Benjamin was reduced to six hundred men and afterwards gave Israel a king, Esther a guardian, and the church an apostle.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth drawing from Ard's tribe is the endurance of a remnant. Judges 20 ends with Benjamin nearly annihilated by the other tribes, six hundred men left at the rock Rimmon and the nation weeping that a tribe was cut off from Israel that day. By any ordinary reckoning Benjamin was finished. Out of that six hundred came Saul the first king, Mordecai who would not bow to Haman, and Saul of Tarsus who said of himself that he was of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews.

The genealogies are what make that visible, which is why they are kept. Ard, who is nothing in the record but a name in two lists, is part of the line that ran through the worst catastrophe in the book of Judges and out the other side. The God who preserves a remnant does it through families whose names no one remembers. Applied to a church in decline or a household that looks spent, the lesson is not optimism about human resilience but confidence in a God who has never yet let the line fail.

pos: n. (proper, a duke of Edom, son of Eliphaz)
etymology: Hebrew Gatam, of uncertain meaning, perhaps a burnt valley. He is the fourth son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, and is named a duke in the land of Edom.
biblical_def: He appears in each of the three rolls of Esau's house: “And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz” (Genesis 36:11); then with his title and his grandmother named: “Duke Korah, duke Gatam, and duke Amalek: these are the dukes that came of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these were the sons of Adah” (Genesis 36:16); and in the Chronicler's condensed version: “The sons of Eliphaz; Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek” (1 Chronicles 1:36). The list he stands in is one of the most consequential in the Old Testament, because Amalek stands in it too. Genesis 36 exists to show that God kept his word to Rebekah that two nations were in her womb. Edom became a nation with dukes and kings while Israel was still a family in Egypt, and Malachi ends the Old Testament's reckoning with it: Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob (Malachi 1:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a son of Eliphaz and a duke of Edom, of the sons of Adah.
webster_full: DUKE, n. In Scripture, the chief of a family or tribe among the Edomites; a leader.
EDOM, n. The country and posterity of Esau, south and east of the Dead sea; a perpetual adversary of Israel.
ADAH, n. One of the wives of Esau, and separately, one of the two wives of Lamech in Genesis 4.
ELECTION, n. In theology, the choice of persons to eternal life; divine choice; predestination.
REPROBATE, a. Abandoned in sin; lost to virtue or grace; not enduring proof or trial.
scriptures: Genesis 36:11
And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz.
Genesis 36:16
Duke Korah, duke Gatam, and duke Amalek: these are the dukes that came of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these were the sons of Adah.
1 Chronicles 1:36
The sons of Eliphaz; Teman, and Omar, Zephi, and Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna, and Amalek.
Malachi 1:2
I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us? Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob,
corruption_summary: The doctrine of God's sovereign choice is felt as the hardest thing in Scripture, and Genesis 36 is where the Bible spends a whole chapter documenting the greatness of the line that was passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: It is worth being honest about how uncomfortable this material is. Genesis 36 is Esau's chapter: dukes by name, kings in succession, a settled land, real greatness. Gatam is one of those dukes. And Malachi, looking back over the whole history, says Was not Esau Jacob's brother? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob (Malachi 1:2), and hated Esau, which Paul quotes in Romans 9 to establish that God's purpose according to election stands not of works but of him that calleth. Scripture does not soften this and neither should we; it grounds the whole of salvation in God's free mercy rather than in anything found in the creature.

Two things keep the doctrine from being read as cruelty. The first is that the passing over is judicial, not capricious: Esau despised his birthright, Hebrews calls him profane, and Obadiah's oracle against Edom is a catalogue of pride and violence against a brother. The second is that the doctrine is given to comfort. Paul sets it in a chapter that begins with his own great heaviness for his kinsmen and ends with a remnant saved; and the practical use the confessions make of election is assurance, humility and diligence — never speculation about another man's standing before God.

pos: n. (proper, one addressed by Agur; also a Benjamite)
etymology: Hebrew Iythiyel, commonly read as God is with me. The name appears twice: in a Benjamite pedigree in Nehemiah, and at the head of the last-but-one chapter of Proverbs, as one of the two men Agur spake unto.
biblical_def: The Benjamite appears in the list of those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the return: “And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah” (Nehemiah 11:7). The famous occurrence opens Proverbs 30: “The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal” (Proverbs 30:1). Nothing more is told of either hearer. What follows is one of the most remarkable passages in the wisdom books: a man who confesses himself more brutish than any man and without the understanding of a man, who asks What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?, who declares every word of God pure and warns against adding to his words, and who prays to be given neither poverty nor riches.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the two men to whom Agur the son of Jakeh spake his prophecy, and as a Benjamite in Nehemiah 11.
webster_full: PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come; in Scripture, also a burden or oracle.
BRUTISH, a. Resembling a brute or beast; insensible; stupid; unfeeling; ignorant.
PURE, a. Separate from all heterogeneous or extraneous matter; clear; unmingled; free from moral defilement.
AGUR, n. The son of Jakeh, the author of the thirtieth chapter of Proverbs.
CONVENIENT, a. Fit; suitable; proper; adapted to use or to wants; as, food convenient for me.
scriptures: Proverbs 30:1
The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal,
Nehemiah 11:7
And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jesaiah.
Proverbs 30:5
Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
Proverbs 30:8
Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
corruption_summary: Confidence is the currency of modern teaching, and the chapter addressed to Ithiel opens with a teacher confessing he is more brutish than any man — and then speaks with more authority than any confident man could.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 30 is addressed to Ithiel and Ucal, and it begins where almost no modern instruction would dare: Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man. I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy. Then a series of questions no man can answer — who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? — and at the end, What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell? The teacher establishes his authority by confessing the limit of his knowledge, which is the opposite of how authority is usually claimed.

What he is certain about is the word: Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him. Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. And what he asks for is moderation: neither poverty nor riches, lest he be full and deny God, or poor and steal and take the name of his God in vain. A man who knows how little he knows, who will not add a syllable to Scripture, and who fears prosperity as much as want — that is the teacher Ithiel got, and the church could use more of them.
